title: Best Fruits for a Hangover: What Helps, What Backfires
excerpt: Which fruits help a hangover? An honest ranking of watermelon, bananas, kiwi, berries, citrus, and more, which fruits backfire, and what fruit can't fix.
metaDescription: The best fruits for a hangover, ranked: watermelon, bananas, kiwi, berries and more. What each helps with, which backfire, and what fruit cannot fix.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** no fruit cures a hangover, but several are genuinely good choices the morning after. Watermelon, bananas, oranges, kiwi, berries, and Asian pears all help in ordinary ways: they bring water, some easy-to-digest sugar for a body that may be running low, potassium, vitamin C, and fiber, and they're often the only thing a queasy stomach can face. What fruit can't do is speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol, undo a bad night's sleep, or switch off the inflammation behind the headache and the "poisoned" feeling. This guide ranks the best fruits for a hangover by what they actually offer, flags the ones that can backfire (citrus on a burning stomach, grapefruit with certain medicines, a big bowl of dried fruit), and covers whether eating fruit before or during drinking makes any difference.

**The quick rules:** If your stomach is upset, start small with something mild and watery, like watermelon, a banana, or a few slices of melon, and sip water alongside it. If you have heartburn, skip the citrus and pineapple for now. Pair fruit with something that has protein or fat (eggs, yogurt, toast with peanut butter) so the sugar doesn't hit all at once. Don't count on fruit juice alone to rehydrate you after vomiting or diarrhea; an oral rehydration drink does that job better.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover from a night out should be clearly improving by the afternoon or evening and gone within about a day. **Get medical help if** you can't keep fluids down for many hours, you're vomiting repeatedly or see blood, you feel faint or very dizzy when you stand, you have severe stomach pain that doesn't ease, your heart is pounding or skipping in a way that doesn't settle, or you're confused or hard to wake. Shaking, sweating, and anxiety that start a day or two after you stop drinking can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, and that needs a doctor, not a fruit bowl. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning (slow or irregular breathing, cold or bluish skin, seizures, can't be woken), call 911.

## Does Fruit Actually Help a Hangover? What It Can and Can't Do

To judge any hangover food fairly, it helps to know what's actually making you feel bad. Researchers now think a hangover is driven by several things at once:

- **The immune system's inflammatory response.** Hungover people show raised levels of inflammatory signaling molecules, and this lines up with the achy, foggy, flu-like feeling.
- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into this toxic by-product before breaking it down further.
- **Poor-quality sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments the second half of the night.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol inflames the stomach lining and increases acid, which feeds nausea.
- **Fluid loss and, for some people, low blood sugar.** Alcohol makes you urinate more, and it interferes with the liver's ability to release stored sugar.

Fruit touches the last two items on that list and, a little, the stomach. It does very little for the first three, which is why no fruit, however healthy, will make a bad hangover disappear. There is no good evidence that any whole fruit shortens a hangover or makes it measurably milder, and very few studies have tested fruit for hangovers at all.

### Where fruit genuinely earns its place

- **Water you can eat.** Many fruits are 80 to 90-plus percent water. If drinking a big glass of water makes you gag, eating watery fruit is a gentler way to get fluid in.
- **Easy carbohydrate.** If your blood sugar dipped overnight, the natural sugars in fruit are quick to absorb. Researchers have found that blood sugar doesn't line up neatly with how bad a hangover feels, so this isn't a cure, but shaky, weak, "I need to eat something" feelings often ease once you get some food in.
- **Potassium.** Bananas, melons, kiwi, oranges, and avocados are good sources. One night of drinking doesn't usually drain potassium in a meaningful way, but if you've been vomiting or had diarrhea, you really have lost some, and food plus fluids helps you replace it. Our post on [bananas for a hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover) goes deeper on the potassium story.
- **Vitamin C and other antioxidants.** Alcohol metabolism creates oxidative stress, and fruit is full of compounds that fight it in the lab. Whether eating them the morning after changes how you feel is unproven. Still, a 2019 survey study by researchers at Utrecht University linked better overall diet quality (including some vitamins and minerals) with less severe hangovers, which is one more reason a real breakfast beats an empty stomach.
- **Gentleness.** Plain, cool, mildly sweet fruit is one of the easiest foods to get down when you're nauseous.

### The fructose question

You may read that fructose, the main sugar in fruit, helps your body burn alcohol faster. This idea comes from older studies, some of which found that large doses of fructose sped up alcohol clearance a little, while others found little or no effect. The amounts used were often far more than you'd get from a piece of fruit, and by the morning after, most or all of the alcohol is usually gone anyway. There is no good evidence that eating fruit lowers your blood alcohol in a way that matters, and it doesn't make you safe to drive.

## The Best Fruits for a Hangover, Ranked by What They Offer

None of these is a cure. They're ranked by how useful they are for the problems you're most likely to have the morning after: dehydration, an empty tank, and an unsettled stomach.

### 1. Watermelon: the best all-rounder for thirst

Watermelon is about 92 percent water, it's cool and mild, and it contains some potassium and natural sugar. For a dry-mouthed, mildly queasy morning, a few cold slices are about as easy as food gets. It's light on fiber, so it won't sit heavily. Our [watermelon for hangover](/never-hungover/watermelon-for-hangover) guide goes deeper.

**Watch for:** on its own it's not much of a meal, and a big bowl can upset a sensitive gut for some people because of its fructose. Pair it with something more substantial once your stomach settles.

### 2. Bananas: the gentlest on an upset stomach

Bananas are soft, bland, and easy to digest, which is why they're a staple of the "bland diet" doctors suggest after stomach upsets. A medium banana has a little over 400 mg of potassium and around 25 to 30 grams of carbohydrate. That makes a banana a solid first food if you've been sick or you can't face anything else. Sliced on toast with peanut butter, it becomes a proper breakfast with protein and fat to slow the sugar down.

**Watch for:** if you have kidney disease or take a medicine that raises potassium (some blood pressure drugs, for example), check with your doctor about high-potassium foods.

### 3. Kiwi: lots of vitamin C in a small package

One kiwi gives you roughly as much vitamin C as a medium orange, along with potassium and fiber, but it's less acidic-tasting for many people. Kiwi also contains an enzyme called actinidin that helps break down protein, which may be part of why some people find it easy on digestion. There's no hangover research on kiwi specifically; it's simply a nutrient-dense, easy option.

**Watch for:** some people have kiwi allergies, which can cause an itchy mouth or worse. If kiwi has ever made your mouth tingle, skip it.

### 4. Asian (Korean) pears: the one fruit with a little hangover research

Asian pears are crisp, juicy, and mild. They're also the only fruit on this list with a small amount of research aimed squarely at hangovers. A small study by Australian researchers, presented in 2013, found that people who drank Korean pear juice before drinking reported milder hangovers on some measures than people who drank a placebo. It was small, it tested juice taken *before* drinking rather than fruit eaten the morning after, and it hasn't been convincingly repeated. So it's interesting, not settled. Our deep dive on [Korean pear juice for hangovers](/never-hungover/korean-pear-juice-hangover) covers what that study did and didn't show.

**Watch for:** pears are high in fructose and sorbitol, which can cause bloating or loose stools in people sensitive to them.

### 5. Berries: antioxidants and fiber without much sugar

Strawberries, blueberries, raspberries, and blackberries are rich in vitamin C and plant compounds called polyphenols, and they're relatively low in sugar. Lab studies suggest some berry compounds can blunt oxidative stress, but that hasn't been shown to translate into a better morning after drinking. They're best stirred into yogurt or oatmeal, which turns them into a balanced breakfast.

**Watch for:** the seeds and fiber in raspberries and blackberries can be a bit much for a very upset stomach. Blueberries are usually gentler.

### 6. Oranges and other citrus: good vitamin C, but hard on heartburn

A medium orange provides about 70 mg of vitamin C, plus potassium and a lot of water, and many people crave something tart and cold the morning after. If your stomach feels fine, an orange is a good choice. The problem is acid. Alcohol relaxes the valve between your stomach and esophagus and increases stomach acid, so if you're already dealing with reflux, citrus can make the burning worse. See our post on [orange juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/orange-juice-for-hangover) for the juice-specific pros and cons.

**Watch for:** heartburn, sour stomach, or a raw throat from vomiting. In those cases, choose banana or melon instead.

### 7. Avocado: the most filling option

Yes, avocado is a fruit, and it's a useful one here. It has more potassium per serving than a banana, healthy fats, and fiber, and it's low in sugar. On toast with an egg, it's one of the more balanced hangover breakfasts you can make. The fat slows digestion, which helps keep you full and avoids a sugar spike and crash.

**Watch for:** fatty foods sit longer in the stomach, so if you're actively nauseous, wait until things settle.

### 8. Cantaloupe and honeydew: watermelon's quieter cousins

Melons are mostly water, mild-flavored, and provide potassium and, in cantaloupe's case, vitamin C and vitamin A. They're another easy choice when you want something cool and light.

### 9. Coconut (water, not the flesh)

Coconut water is a fruit product rather than a whole fruit, but it belongs in this conversation because it's so often reached for. It's high in potassium and low in sodium, which is the opposite of what you lose most of when you sweat or have diarrhea. It's fine as a pleasant drink, but it isn't a better rehydrator than an oral rehydration solution. We break down the details in [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover).

### Honorable mentions

- **Grapes:** watery and easy to eat, but sugary, so pair them with protein.
- **Pineapple:** contains bromelain, an enzyme with some anti-inflammatory research, but there's no good evidence it helps a hangover. It's also acidic, so it's a poor pick with heartburn.
- **Tomatoes:** botanically a fruit, and a classic base for hangover drinks. They bring water, potassium, and a little sodium if salted. Skip the vodka in the Bloody Mary; drinking more alcohol only postpones the hangover.
- **Dates and dried fruit:** concentrated sugar and fiber with very little water. A few are fine; a big handful on an empty, irritated stomach can trigger cramps or loose stools.

## Fruits and Fruit Habits That Can Backfire

Most fruit is a safe bet, but a few situations call for care.

### Citrus, pineapple, and acidic fruit with heartburn

If your chest or upper stomach is burning, acidic fruit and juices can add fuel to it. Choose low-acid fruit (banana, melon, pear, papaya) until it settles. If reflux after drinking is a regular problem, our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) explains what helps.

### Grapefruit with medications

Grapefruit and grapefruit juice block an enzyme in your gut that breaks down many common medicines, which can push blood levels of the drug higher than intended. The list includes some statins, some blood pressure medicines, some anti-anxiety and sleep drugs, and others. If you take any regular prescription, check the label or ask your pharmacist before adding grapefruit, hangover or not. This interaction has nothing to do with alcohol, but people often reach for juice the morning after without thinking about it.

### Big servings of high-fructose fruit when your gut is upset

Alcohol can already loosen your bowels. Large amounts of fructose and sorbitol, found in apples, pears, mangoes, cherries, and dried fruit, and especially in juices, can make diarrhea worse in people who don't absorb these sugars well. If your gut is already in trouble, eat small portions and favor bananas and melon. More on this in our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking).

### Fruit juice as your only fluid

Juice is concentrated sugar with most of the fiber removed, and it's low in sodium. After heavy vomiting or diarrhea, plain juice doesn't replace what you've lost very well, and a lot of sugar on its own can draw water into the gut. Dilute juice with water if you want it, and use an oral rehydration solution when you've lost a lot of fluid. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) walks through the options.

### Fruit in place of a real meal

Fruit on its own is low in protein and fat, so the sugar is absorbed quickly and you may feel hungry and shaky again an hour later. Treat fruit as one part of a hangover breakfast, not the whole thing.

## Is Fruit Better Before, During, or After Drinking?

### Before drinking

Eating before you drink slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which lowers your peak blood alcohol level. Meals with protein, fat, and fiber do this best, because they keep food in your stomach longer. Fruit alone empties from the stomach fairly quickly, so it offers only modest protection. A banana or apple is better than nothing, but a proper meal is much better. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers the evidence.

### During drinking

Fruit garnishes don't change much, but snacking does help. Having food on hand, including fruit, slows your drinking and your absorption, and watery fruit adds a little fluid. Alternating each drink with a glass of water matters more than anything you put in the glass.

### After drinking (the next morning)

This is where fruit helps most, as a gentle, hydrating part of breakfast. A reasonable order of operations:

1. Sip water or an electrolyte drink first.
2. Start with a small portion of mild fruit (banana, watermelon, melon) to test your stomach.
3. Once that stays down, add protein: eggs, Greek yogurt, or nut butter on toast.
4. Save acidic fruit and big servings of sweet fruit for later in the day if your stomach is sensitive.

## Three Easy Hangover Fruit Combos

You don't need a recipe, but these pairings cover hydration, carbohydrate, and protein in one go:

- **Banana and peanut butter on toast.** Gentle, filling, and quick. Add a glass of water.
- **Greek yogurt with blueberries and a sliced kiwi.** Protein, vitamin C, and a bit of fiber, cool and easy to eat.
- **A simple smoothie:** banana, a handful of frozen berries or mango, plain yogurt, a little milk or water, and a pinch of salt if you've been sweating or sick. Sipping a smoothie slowly is easier than eating when you're nauseous. If nausea is the main problem, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) and the post on [ginger for a hangover](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) have more ideas.

For the full picture of what to eat beyond fruit, see our guide to the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover).

## What Fruit Won't Fix

It's worth being plain about the limits:

- **Fruit doesn't sober you up.** Only time clears alcohol from your blood. If you drank late, you may still be over the limit in the morning regardless of what you eat.
- **Fruit doesn't fix poor sleep.** The tired, foggy feeling from fragmented sleep needs rest.
- **Fruit doesn't cancel out heavy drinking.** The most reliable way to have a better morning is to drink less, drink more slowly, eat a real meal first, and alternate with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through the habits with the best evidence.

## Where DHM Fits In

Fruit is about recovery. Some people also look at supplements taken around drinking. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis) that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research is in animals and lab settings, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone or makes heavy drinking safe. If you want to try it alongside the basics of food, water, and moderation, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicine, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

The best fruits for a hangover are the ones your stomach can handle and that give you water and easy energy: watermelon and other melons for thirst, bananas for a sore stomach, kiwi and berries for vitamin C, avocado for staying power, and oranges if heartburn isn't an issue. Asian pears have a small, early study behind them, but it's not strong evidence. Eat fruit alongside water and some protein, go easy on acidic and high-fructose fruit if your gut is upset, and check before mixing grapefruit with any regular medication. Fruit will help you feel a bit more human. It won't erase the night before.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best fruit for a hangover?**

There isn't one best fruit, because none of them cures a hangover. For most people, watermelon is the best all-rounder for thirst, and bananas are the best for an upset stomach. Kiwi and berries are good for vitamin C, and avocado is the most filling. Choose whatever your stomach can handle, and pair it with water and some protein.

**Are bananas or watermelon better for a hangover?**

They do slightly different jobs. Watermelon is about 92 percent water, so it's better when you're mainly thirsty. Bananas are more filling, gentler on a queasy stomach, and higher in potassium, so they're better if you've been sick or need something more substantial. Having both is fine.

**Is orange juice good for a hangover?**

It can be, if your stomach is fine. Orange juice gives you fluid, vitamin C, potassium, and quick sugar. But it's acidic, so it can worsen heartburn after drinking, and it's a lot of sugar on its own. Dilute it with water, drink it with food, and switch to a low-acid fruit if you have reflux.

**Does fruit help your body get rid of alcohol faster?**

Not in a way that matters. Some older studies found that large doses of fructose slightly sped up alcohol clearance, while others found little or no effect. There is no good evidence that eating fruit lowers your blood alcohol meaningfully, and it won't make you safe to drive. Only time clears alcohol.

**Should I eat fruit before drinking?**

Eating anything before drinking is better than drinking on an empty stomach, because food slows alcohol absorption. But fruit leaves the stomach fairly quickly, so it offers only modest protection. A meal with protein, fat, and fiber does a much better job. Fruit is a fine addition to that meal.

**Which fruits should I avoid with a hangover?**

If you have heartburn, avoid citrus, pineapple, and other acidic fruit until it settles. If your gut is upset, go easy on large servings of high-fructose fruit, dried fruit, and fruit juice, which can make diarrhea worse. If you take any regular medication, check with a pharmacist before having grapefruit, which interacts with many common drugs.

**Is coconut water better than fruit for a hangover?**

It's a different thing. Coconut water is high in potassium but low in sodium, so it's not as good as an oral rehydration solution after vomiting or diarrhea. Whole fruit brings fiber and more nutrients. Either is fine as part of recovery, but neither is a cure.

**Does Korean pear juice really prevent hangovers?**

There's a small study, presented by Australian researchers in 2013, that found Korean pear juice taken before drinking eased some hangover symptoms compared with a placebo. It was small, tested juice before drinking rather than fruit afterward, and hasn't been convincingly repeated. It's an interesting lead, but there is no good evidence that it reliably prevents hangovers.
